_comment: The standard workload. Targets the experiments realm, which ships in the
repo as packages/experiments-realm (332 instances across 142 modules) and
exists in every deployed environment, so it is the one realm everybody can
point at. Run this to get a number comparable to someone else's.
WHAT COMPARABILITY MEANS HERE. The realm in the repo and a realm deployed
from it are not guaranteed to hold the same instances, and nothing keeps
them in step. Instance counts measured on a deployed experiments realm
against the same types counted in packages/experiments-realm:
deployed   in repo
Spec                           117        28
FileDefFormatPreview            37        37
Author                          30         5
Model                           30        30
CardListing                     26         0
Company                         25         5
SprintTask                      25        15
CRMTask                         24        13
So these queries give comparable numbers across runs against THE SAME
TARGET — before and after a change, on one environment. They do not make
two targets comparable to each other; compare each against its own earlier
run. On a realm cloned from the repo, CardListing returns nothing and the
other shapes are smaller; that is the realm differing, not a regression.
The types are the realm's highest-count instance types, chosen by count
rather than by interest, so the set tracks where the cost actually is.
Re-derive against whatever you are testing with --derive-workload when the
realm has moved on.
The queries are unbounded: every instance of the type, with its included[]
closure assembled. That is the shape this harness exists to measure.
--derive-workload bounds its queries at 20 by default, so a derived run and
this one are not comparable to each other either.
The writers post an Author, which is in the read set, so each write
invalidates a query the readers are running. Point this at a realm you are
willing to dirty — a clone made by setup-realm.ts — or pass --writers 0 for
a read-only run.
